## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, we rank the enriched biological pathways associated with depression on the basis of statistical significance and biological relevance. Notably, immune and inflammatory pathways are strongly represented, including receptor complex (Gene Ontology: 0043235, P < 2.05 × 10−9), Signaling by Interleukins (Reactome: R-HSA-449147, P < 1.68 × 10−3), Other interleukin signaling (Reactome: R-HSA-449836, P < 1.41 × 10−2), Cytokines and inflammatory response (WikiPathways: 530, P < 1.81 × 10−4), and Rheumatoid arthritis (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 05323, P < 3.38 × 10−6). Taken together, the prominence of these terms suggests that inflammatory signaling may represent a major component of the observed enrichment pattern. These findings are consistent with extensive literature indicating that depression is frequently accompanied by chronic low-grade inflammation, elevated interleukin signaling, altered cytokine balance, and abnormal immune receptor activity, all of which can influence neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and stress responsiveness.

Building on this inflammatory profile, transcriptional regulatory signals also emerge prominently, particularly Factor: p53; motif: NGRCATGYCCAGRCATGYCY; match class: 1 (Transcription factor database: M10023_1, P < 1.10 × 10−2) and Factor: interferon regulatory factor; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (Transcription factor database: M08887_1, P < 4.06 × 10−2). This pattern suggests that stress-response, inflammatory, and apoptosis-related transcriptional programs may contribute to depression biology. In the literature, p53 signaling has been linked to neuronal injury, cellular senescence, and stress-induced molecular changes, while interferon regulatory factor activity is closely connected to innate immune activation and interferon-driven inflammatory states that have been associated with depressive symptoms.

A related extension of these regulatory signals is the enrichment of pathways involved in lipid handling and intracellular transport. Specifically, additional enrichment of regulation of lipid metabolic process (Gene Ontology: 0019216, P < 1.66 × 10−2), cargo receptor activity (Gene Ontology: 0038024, P < 2.77 × 10−5), and late endosome (Gene Ontology: 0005770, P < 1.63 × 10−2) points to altered membrane composition, intracellular trafficking, and vesicular processing. These processes are highly relevant because lipid metabolism affects membrane fluidity, receptor signaling, and inflammatory mediator production, while endosomal and cargo-sorting pathways regulate receptor turnover and cytokine signaling. Such mechanisms have been increasingly implicated in depression, particularly in relation to synaptic dysfunction, immune signaling, and cellular stress adaptation.

Extending from intracellular processes to tissue-associated biology, the enrichment pattern also highlights signals related to mucosal immunity and intestinal function. Specifically, the enrichment of Intestinal immune network for immunoglobulin A production (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes: 04672, P < 1.02 × 10−4), together with tissue-linked signals such as Colon; goblet cells [high] (Human Protein Atlas: 0130893, P < 4.82 × 10−8) and Colon; goblet cells [greater than or equal to medium] (Human Protein Atlas: 0130892, P < 4.69 × 10−8), suggests a possible contribution of mucosal immunity and gut-barrier biology to depression. This interpretation is supported by growing evidence for a gut-brain axis in depression, in which intestinal immune activation, epithelial maintenance, and altered host-microbe interactions can promote systemic inflammation and affect brain function. Overall, these top-ranked pathways support a model in which depression may involve convergent disturbances in inflammatory signaling, transcriptional stress responses, receptor-mediated communication, lipid and vesicular biology, and gut-associated immune regulation.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways. To maintain continuity with the overview above, the analysis will move from the strongest inflammatory and immune-related signals toward the broader regulatory, trafficking, and tissue-associated patterns that may also be relevant.


### Factor: IRF; motif: NNGAAANTGAAANN; match class: 1 (TF:M08887_1) 

Interferon regulatory factor pathway activity refers to transcriptional control mediated by members of the interferon regulatory factor family binding to a deoxyribonucleic acid sequence motif characterized here as NNGAAANTGAAANN. Interferon regulatory factors are sequence-specific transcription factors that are central regulators of innate immune signaling, antiviral defense, inflammatory cytokine production, antigen presentation, and immune cell differentiation. These factors are typically activated downstream of pattern-recognition receptor signaling, interferon receptor signaling, and other cytokine-triggered pathways, after which they translocate to the nucleus and bind interferon-stimulated response element-like motifs to induce or repress target genes. Depending on cellular context, interferon regulatory factors coordinate expression of type one interferons, interferon-stimulated genes, chemokines, major histocompatibility complex-related genes, and additional immune effector programs. Because immune activation, neuroinflammation, microglial responses, blood-brain barrier perturbation, and stress-associated cytokine signaling have all been implicated in the pathophysiology of depression, transcriptional programs governed by interferon regulatory factors are biologically plausible contributors to depression-related molecular changes. In particular, this pathway may provide a mechanistic link between peripheral immune stimulation and central nervous system inflammatory signaling, altered synaptic plasticity, impaired neurogenesis, and behavioral changes relevant to depressive symptomatology.

With this biological context in mind, it is important to distinguish mechanistic plausibility from direct evidence derived from the supplied literature set. No pathway-specific publications were provided in the input, so there is no direct citation-supported evidence set available here to establish a depression-specific role for the interferon regulatory factor motif-defined pathway. Nevertheless, from a biological standpoint, the pathway appears plausibly related to depression because interferon regulatory factors orchestrate innate immune and interferon-driven transcriptional responses, and depression has repeatedly been associated with heightened inflammatory tone, cytokine dysregulation, and immune-to-brain communication. Within this framework, activation of interferon regulatory factor-dependent gene expression could promote production of inflammatory mediators and interferon-responsive genes in peripheral immune cells and central nervous system-resident immune populations, thereby contributing to neuroinflammatory states that influence monoamine metabolism, glutamatergic signaling, synaptic remodeling, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, and neuronal plasticity. Such processes are highly relevant to core features of depression, including anhedonia, low mood, fatigue, cognitive dysfunction, and stress sensitivity. However, because the publication list is empty, any asserted connection remains inferential rather than directly supported by the supplied literature, and pathway involvement in depression should therefore be regarded as a mechanistically reasonable hypothesis requiring validation through transcriptomic, epigenomic, genetic, or functional studies that specifically link interferon regulatory factor activity to depressive phenotypes.

A quantitative enrichment result further supports the relevance of considering this pathway in the present dataset. There were 127 depression-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of interferon regulatory factor pathway activity, indicating a substantial immune-related transcriptional program within the analyzed protein set. This pathway is defined by sequence-specific binding of interferon regulatory factor family members to the deoxyribonucleic acid motif NNGAAANTGAAANN and regulates transcriptional outputs that include type one interferons, interferon-stimulated genes, inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, antigen presentation machinery, and immune cell differentiation programs. In the context of depression, the enrichment of 127 proteins is biologically notable because it quantitatively supports a strong connection between depression-associated molecular changes and immune signaling processes that have been linked to neuroinflammation, microglial activation, blood-brain barrier dysfunction, altered neurogenesis, impaired synaptic plasticity, and stress-responsive cytokine signaling. Collectively, the size of the enriched set, comprising 127 proteins, suggests that interferon regulatory factor-mediated transcription is not a marginal feature but rather a prominent component of the functional landscape associated with depression.

To complement this enrichment result, the network-level organization of the 127 proteins provides an additional view of their potential functional interrelationships. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for the 127 enriched proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage can be accessed through the embedded link for interactive exploration of network connectivity and functional relationships.

Building on this network and enrichment context, the following section introduces several significant proteins identified during the function enrichment analysis and discusses their possible relevance in a more focused manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CD14 is among the most compelling proteins in this list for relevance to depression because it sits at the interface of innate immunity, microbial sensing, and cytokine induction. A substantial body of depression research implicates chronic low-grade inflammation, exaggerated innate immune activation, and altered gut-microbe/host immune interactions in symptom generation and persistence. By facilitating lipopolysaccharide and toll-like receptor 4 signaling and downstream nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-driven inflammatory cascades, CD14 provides a mechanistic link to the elevated peripheral inflammatory markers frequently observed in major depressive disorder. Its additional role in responses to microbial lipoproteins and modified lipids further supports its relevance to neuroimmune models of depression, in which peripheral inflammatory signaling can influence microglial activation, sickness behavior, anhedonia, and altered monoamine and glutamate metabolism.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712) 

Extending this immune-regulatory theme, CHI3L1 is notable because it integrates inflammation, tissue remodeling, and stress adaptation, all of which are increasingly implicated in depression. Its capacity to regulate dendritic cells, macrophage polarization, inflammatory apoptosis, and epithelial cytokine production suggests a broad immunomodulatory role that could shape systemic inflammatory tone. In depression, immune dysregulation is not limited to classic pro-inflammatory cytokines but also includes altered innate immune cell phenotypes and maladaptive stress responses in peripheral tissues. CHI3L1 therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of immune-brain communication, particularly in patients with inflammatory, metabolic, or stress-related depressive phenotypes.

In a related counter-regulatory direction, IL18BP is highly relevant because it counter-regulates interleukin 18, a cytokine strongly linked to inflammatory activation and stress-related pathology. Since inflammatory cytokines are repeatedly associated with depressive symptoms, especially anhedonia, fatigue, and treatment resistance, proteins that buffer cytokine activity are of particular interest. By neutralizing interleukin 18 and dampening early T helper type 1 responses, IL18BP may influence the magnitude of systemic and possibly neuroinflammatory signaling. This makes it biologically meaningful in depression models centered on immune overactivation and may also be relevant to resilience mechanisms that protect against inflammation-associated mood disturbance.

A similar immunoregulatory perspective also highlights LGALS1, which stands out because it modulates adaptive immune homeostasis at several levels, including T-cell survival and T helper type 17 differentiation. Depression has been associated not only with innate immune activation but also with altered T-cell phenotypes and skewed inflammatory set points. The ability of LGALS1 to induce T-cell apoptosis and suppress T helper type 17 differentiation suggests a potentially important immunoregulatory role in limiting chronic inflammatory states relevant to mood disorders. Moreover, galectins have broader effects on cell-cell communication and stress biology, making LGALS1 a plausible contributor to the immune-endocrine disturbances observed in depression.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

Alongside these balancing mechanisms, LILRB4 is particularly interesting because it is a broad inhibitory regulator of immune signaling pathways, including receptor tyrosine kinases, cytokine pathways, and cyclic guanosine monophosphate-adenosine monophosphate synthase-stimulator of interferon genes-related innate immune signaling. Depression has increasingly been conceptualized as a disorder involving aberrant immune set-point regulation rather than simple cytokine excess alone. In that context, LILRB4 may be relevant as a molecular brake whose altered activity could influence inflammatory threshold, antigen-presenting cell behavior, and downstream neuroimmune consequences. Its additional metabolic regulatory role is also noteworthy, given the close relationship between depression, metabolic dysfunction, and systemic inflammation.[PubMed:9528781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9528781) [PubMed:10026201](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10026201) [PubMed:33990399](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33990399) 

Shifting from immune inhibition toward neurovascular and reparative biology, MDK is one of the strongest candidates in this dataset because it bridges neurodevelopment, neurorepair, inflammation, and vascular biology. It promotes neural precursor survival, neuronal migration, and tissue regeneration, while also modulating inflammatory cell recruitment and anti-apoptotic signaling through mitogen-activated protein kinase and protein kinase B pathways. These functions are highly relevant to contemporary models of depression, which emphasize impaired neuroplasticity, altered neuroimmune signaling, and cerebrovascular dysfunction. MDK-induced vascular endothelial growth factor A expression and nitric oxide signaling are especially notable, as both angiogenic and endothelial pathways have been implicated in stress susceptibility and antidepressant response. Thus, MDK could plausibly connect inflammatory injury responses with adaptive or maladaptive neural remodeling in depression.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) [PubMed:1768439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1768439) 

This neurovascular emphasis continues with CCN3, which is highly relevant to depression because it intersects with Notch signaling, hypoxia-related pathways, angiogenesis, and neural and glial differentiation. Depression has been linked to impaired neurogenesis, altered glial support, and dysregulated cellular plasticity in corticolimbic circuits. CCN3 may influence these processes through effects on differentiation and apoptosis, while its interaction with hypoxia inducible factor 1 subunit alpha-related biology suggests possible relevance to cellular stress adaptation and metabolic stress. Its anti-angiogenic actions are also important, since vascular and endothelial dysfunction are increasingly recognized as contributors to mood disorders, particularly in inflammatory and late-life depression.

A closely related vascular mechanism is represented by DDAH1, which is important because it directly controls nitric oxide bioavailability by degrading endogenous nitric oxide synthase inhibitors. Nitric oxide signaling is relevant to depression through several mechanisms, including endothelial function, neurovascular coupling, synaptic plasticity, oxidative stress, and inflammatory signaling. Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability has been associated with vascular dysfunction and may contribute to the cerebrovascular and metabolic abnormalities seen in subsets of depressed patients. Therefore, DDAH1 may represent a mechanistic node linking vascular depression, inflammatory stress, and altered neuronal signaling.

In the same angiogenic framework, COL18A1 is relevant because it is a strong endogenous anti-angiogenic factor that antagonizes vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling. Vascular endothelial growth factor-related pathways are widely implicated in stress resilience, hippocampal plasticity, and antidepressant mechanisms. Consequently, proteins that suppress vascular endothelial growth factor A-driven endothelial and possibly neurovascular responses may influence brain perfusion, blood-brain barrier dynamics, and neuroplastic adaptation. COL18A1 may therefore be especially pertinent in depression subtypes characterized by vascular dysfunction, impaired repair responses, or reduced trophic support.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

This line of reasoning also supports consideration of ACVRL1, which is noteworthy because it links angiogenesis to transforming growth factor beta and mothers against decapentaplegic signaling, both of which are relevant to depression. Transforming growth factor beta pathway abnormalities have been implicated in immune regulation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and neuroplasticity, while endothelial dysfunction and impaired angiogenic signaling are increasingly recognized in mood disorders. As a potent anti-angiogenic factor acting through endothelial mothers against decapentaplegic 1 signaling, ACVRL1 may contribute to altered vascular adaptation and neurovascular health, processes that may be particularly important in chronic stress exposure and treatment-resistant depression.

A broader vasoactive component is suggested by ADM, which is relevant to depression because adrenomedullin is a vasoactive and stress-responsive peptide with established roles in vascular tone, endothelial biology, and systemic homeostasis. Although the provided annotation is concise, its receptor-mediated signaling strongly suggests participation in neurovascular and inflammatory regulation. Given the emerging importance of endothelial dysfunction, autonomic imbalance, and altered stress physiology in depression, ADM may be functionally significant, particularly in patients with comorbid cardiovascular or inflammatory features.

Within this stress-adaptation and vascular context, HSPB6 stands out because it combines stress-protective chaperone activity with vascular and angiogenic functions. Depression is increasingly understood as a multisystem disorder involving stress-induced proteostatic burden, endothelial dysfunction, and elevated cardiovascular risk. HSPB6 may be relevant through its capacity to support cellular resilience under stress and to promote vasorelaxation and angiogenesis, processes that could influence cerebral perfusion and systemic stress adaptation. Its cardioprotective profile is also notable given the strong bidirectional relationship between depression and cardiovascular disease.

Another major regulatory node in this broader tissue-remodeling landscape is TGFBR2, which is highly relevant because transforming growth factor beta signaling is a central regulator of immune suppression, extracellular matrix remodeling, wound repair, and cellular differentiation, all of which have plausible links to depression pathophysiology. Altered transforming growth factor beta signaling may contribute to chronic inflammatory tone, glial and extracellular matrix remodeling, and maladaptive stress responses. The receptor's engagement in both canonical mothers against decapentaplegic signaling and non-canonical apoptotic and epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related pathways suggests broad effects on tissue homeostasis that may extend to the brain and neurovascular unit. This makes TGFBR2 a biologically meaningful candidate in inflammation-associated and stress-related depression.[PubMed:33914044](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33914044) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) 

Returning to adaptive immunity, TNFRSF9 is of interest because it regulates T-cell survival and mitochondrial fitness, two domains increasingly connected to depression biology. Immune activation in depression often includes altered T-cell function, while mitochondrial dysfunction is a recurring theme in fatigue, low energy, and stress vulnerability. By promoting cluster of differentiation 8-positive T-cell persistence and mitochondrial activity, TNFRSF9 may influence the broader immune-metabolic state that shapes neuroimmune communication. It may be particularly relevant in contexts where chronic immune stimulation contributes to depressive symptoms.

A more inflammatory signaling-centered candidate is TNFRSF11A, which is highly pertinent because it is embedded in major inflammatory signaling pathways, including nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activation downstream of tumor necrosis factor, interleukin 1, and interleukin 17 family signals. These pathways are repeatedly implicated in depression, especially in patients with elevated inflammatory biomarkers and somatic symptom burden. Its role in dendritic cell activation and T-cell receptor signaling also indicates broader immune network effects. This protein therefore represents a plausible hub through which peripheral inflammatory stimuli could amplify systemic immune activation and contribute to depression-related neuroinflammatory consequences.[PubMed:11057907](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11057907) [PubMed:18347055](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18347055) [PubMed:19465916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19465916) [PubMed:19713527](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19713527) [PubMed:27746020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27746020) [PubMed:31620128](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31620128) [PubMed:19675569](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19675569) [PubMed:16378096](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16378096) [PubMed:17135271](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17135271) [PubMed:17703191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17703191) [PubMed:12140561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12140561) [PubMed:19825828](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19825828) [PubMed:8837778](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8837778) [PubMed:18093978](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18093978) [PubMed:18758450](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18758450) [PubMed:23514740](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23514740) [PubMed:25907557](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25907557) 

At the intersection of immunity and cellular energetics, RNASET2 is particularly interesting because it links innate immune sensing to ribonucleic acid metabolism and mitochondrial homeostasis. Depression has been associated with both abnormal innate immune activation and mitochondrial dysfunction, and RNASET2 occupies a mechanistic intersection between these domains. By generating ribonucleic acid ligands that activate toll-like receptor 7 and toll-like receptor 8, it may influence inflammatory responses to endogenous or microbial nucleic acids. Its role in mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover further suggests relevance to cellular stress adaptation and immunometabolic signaling, both increasingly important in contemporary models of depression.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512) 

A related, although somewhat more indirect, host-defense perspective is provided by RNASE6, which is relevant because host defense proteins that shape antimicrobial responses may influence the microbiome-immune axis implicated in depression. Altered microbial exposure and barrier-immune interactions are increasingly discussed in mood disorders, particularly in relation to chronic inflammation and sickness behavior. RNASE6 may therefore be important as part of a broader innate immune antimicrobial program that modulates inflammatory burden and host-microbe interactions.[PubMed:15693621](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15693621) [PubMed:25075772](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25075772) 

Bridging immune defense and neural structure, SPON2 is notable because it combines neuronal and innate immune functions. On one hand, it supports neuronal adhesion and outgrowth, which is relevant to neural connectivity and plasticity; on the other, it participates directly in bacterial recognition and macrophage-mediated host defense. This dual role makes SPON2 especially interesting in depression, where both impaired neuroplasticity and altered peripheral immune activation are central themes. It may represent a molecular bridge between extracellular matrix organization, neuronal maintenance, and inflammatory responses to microbial products.

This transition from immune-neural interfaces to more directly neuropsychiatric mechanisms brings attention to GFRA1, which is one of the most directly neuropsychiatrically relevant proteins in the list because it mediates glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor signaling in dopaminergic neurons. Dopamine dysfunction is strongly implicated in anhedonia, motivational deficits, psychomotor slowing, and reward-processing abnormalities in depression. By supporting dopaminergic neuron survival, differentiation, and dopamine uptake through rearranged during transfection activation, GFRA1 may influence mesolimbic and nigrostriatal circuit integrity. This makes it particularly important in biologically informed models of depression centered on impaired reward processing and neurotrophic support.

A complementary synaptic-plasticity perspective is provided by NCS1, which is highly relevant because synaptic plasticity and calcium-dependent signaling are central to current pathophysiological models of depression. Rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms, stress-induced synaptic remodeling, and maladaptive circuit plasticity all converge on calcium signaling and receptor trafficking. NCS1 may influence these processes through regulation of G protein-coupled receptor signaling, phosphoinositide metabolism, and long-term synaptic plasticity. Its role in neuronal differentiation further supports its potential significance in maintaining circuit adaptability under chronic stress.

Within this broader framework of circuit remodeling, YAP1 is noteworthy because erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 signaling has established roles in synaptic development, interneuron function, and neurodevelopmental signaling networks that can affect mood-related circuitry. Although the annotation here is concise, YAP1-mediated activation of erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 suggests possible relevance to cortical inhibitory balance and neuronal plasticity. Since depression is increasingly viewed as a disorder of maladaptive circuit remodeling rather than solely neurotransmitter deficiency, proteins influencing erb-b family signaling may have mechanistic importance.

A more homeostatic and behavioral dimension is suggested by NUCB2, which is relevant because appetite dysregulation, energy imbalance, and autonomic changes are core features of many depressive syndromes. As an anorexigenic factor acting in hypothalamic pathways independently of leptin, NUCB2 may contribute to altered feeding behavior and metabolic symptoms in depression. Its possible vascular effects further connect it to the broader cardiometabolic dimension of mood disorders. This protein is therefore particularly interesting for depressive phenotypes characterized by appetite loss, weight change, and altered homeostatic regulation.

Finally, this symptom-oriented perspective converges with systemic stress signaling in GDF15, which stands out strongly because it is a canonical stress-responsive cytokine-like hormone that drives aversive behavior and appetite suppression via a defined brainstem circuit. These functions overlap with key depressive symptoms, including reduced appetite, weight loss, malaise, and behavioral withdrawal. In addition, GDF15 is induced by diverse stressors, including cancer, cytotoxic drugs, and metformin, making it a broader signal of systemic distress. Its capacity to activate central aversion pathways suggests a plausible contribution to sickness behavior and somatic-affective symptom clusters that overlap with inflammation-associated depression.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391)
